meta.index.desc: From zero to Cloud Engineer: a live terminal, 54 quests, 211 hands-on tasks. Learn Linux, AWS, Terraform, Docker and Kubernetes by typing real commands. Genuinely beginner level.
idx.heroTitle: Learn to become aCloud Engineerby playing.
idx.lead1: Watch a video, take notes, forget it in three days. The familiar loop. Something else happens here: you type the command yourself.
idx.lead2: It's your first day at a startup called Meridian. The only engineer holding the infrastructure up has quit, and you're their replacement. The investor demo is six weeks away.
idx.heroFine: Your first task is typing pwd. If you've never opened a terminal, you're in the right place.
idx.figuresNote: None of it was generated automatically. All 211 tasks were written by hand and are tested on every build — a task whose own solution doesn't pass its check can't ship.
idx.fairTitle:
If you thought it through,
it's right.
idx.fairP1: Most platforms compare your command as text. Put the flags in a different order, add a sudo — it says "wrong". You're not learning; you're memorizing what the editor wrote.
idx.fairP2: CloudQuest actually parses your command: it splits it into segments, tokenizes quote-aware, and checks your intent. The four lines beside this are all from the same task.
idx.claimA.b:
There's a mentor telling you what to type at every step and why you're typing it. Get it wrong three times and the right command arrives free — so you don't get stuck and quit.

Nobody says "go look it up" and leaves you on your own.
idx.claimB.b:
Verification happens on the server. You can't grant yourself a level from the browser console, and the answer key is never sent to the browser at all.

Which means the badge you earn actually means something. Even to yourself.
idx.claimC.b:
Every chapter is an act: the launch, the funding round, the scaling crisis, the 3 a.m. on-call, the security audit. From rookie to Platform Lead.

The learning is centre stage and the drama is behind it — not the other way round.
idx.claimD.h: You can see where you got stuck
idx.claimD.b:
Every attempt is recorded. How many times you missed on which topic, and which chapter slowed you down, sits in your profile.

You don't have to guess what to revise.
idx.sylLead: Eight chapters that unlock in order. Each stands on the one before it. No skipping — because what you skip catches up with you three chapters later.
idx.syl1: The shell, files, permissions, processes, packages and services.
idx.syl2: How packets flow, how you reach a server, how code gets versioned.
idx.syl3: IAM, EC2, VPC, S3 — the core of the cloud.
idx.syl4: Describe your infrastructure in Terraform; stop clicking in the console.
idx.syl5: Package, ship and scale with Docker.
idx.syl6: An automatic build → test → deploy pipeline.
idx.syl7: Logs, metrics, alarms. The system talks; you learn to listen.
idx.syl8: Least privilege, secret management, and the art of not blowing up the bill.

idx.honestTitle: What it is, and what it isn't.
idx.honestLead: Overselling helps nobody. We'd rather you knew now what you'll have in your hands at the end.
idx.isList:
• + Muscle memory for the commands. A shell you can type in without thinking.
  • + A map of cloud concepts: what connects to what.
  • + The place where the fear of the terminal ends.
  • + Solid ground to start a real project from.
idx.isNotList:
• — Certification exam prep (AWS SAA and the like) — different scope.
  • — A real AWS environment. The commands run in a simulated terminal.
  • — A job guarantee. Nobody can offer one; anyone who does isn't telling the truth.
  • — A weekend crash course. This takes 4-6 months.
idx.faq1.q: I've never used a terminal — can I still start?
idx.faq1.a: Yes — that's exactly what it was designed for. The first task is typing pwd. Nova explains what to type and why at every step, and after three wrong tries shows you the right command for free. If you like, take the Terminal 101 tour before you go in.
idx.faq2.q: Do I need a real AWS account? Will I have to pay?
idx.faq2.a: No. You type the commands in CloudQuest's own terminal; no credit card or cloud account is required. We do recommend trying what you learn on a real AWS Free Tier account, but it isn't mandatory.
idx.faq3.q: How long until I'm a Cloud Engineer?
idx.faq3.a: The curriculum is built around a 6-month programme: 8 chapters, 54 quests, 211 hands-on tasks. For someone putting in a few hours a week, 4-6 months is a reasonable range. Let's be honest: this game builds your muscle memory, and you'll need real projects alongside it to be interview-ready.
idx.faq4.a: No. Your progress lives on the server and syncs across all your devices with your account. Verification also happens on the server — nobody can grant themselves a level from the console, so a badge you earned was genuinely earned.
idx.faq5.a: 8 chapters: Terminal & Linux, Networking & Git, AWS Core, Infrastructure as Code, Containers, CI/CD, Observability, and Security & Cost. Plus 6 advanced labs: Network Ops, Scripting, Docker Deep Dive, Terraform Pro, Ansible and Kubernetes.
idx.faq6.a: It's free for now. You do need an account — so your progress can follow you between devices and be verified.
idx.finalBody: No install, no card. Create an account, open the terminal, type pwd. The rest follows on its own.
